paragraphs.text: Hyposulfatemia with skeletal dysplasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SLC13A1. Patients come to medical attention because of short stature, scoliosis, and/or skeletal dysplasia. The dysplasia ranges from multiple epiphyseal to spondyloepiphyseal and spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia. Loss of renal sulfate reabsorption causes reduced plasma sulfate and increased urinary sulfate excretion, which can serve as a measurable biomarker (van de Kamp et al., 2023; Tise et al., 2025).

paragraphs.text: van de Kamp et al. (2023) reported a Dutch boy who was the only child of nonconsanguineous parents. He presented at 4 months of age with enlarged knees that could not fully extend; his length and head circumference were normal. A skeletal survey at 6 months showed ovoid vertebral bodies, spiky widening of the metaphyses, irregular tarsal bones, slight rib flaring, and somewhat small epiphyses, which were more noticeable at 4 years. The skull and pelvis were normal, as were serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D3. The radiologic abnormalities improved with age. By 11 years, only flattening of the cervical vertebral bodies and irregular lumbar vertebral endplates remained.

paragraphs.text: At 12 years, the patient of van de Kamp et al. (2023) had enlarged knees and elbows, reduced movement in the lumbar spine and knees, winged scapulae, finger hypermobility, and flat feet. His height was normal (+1 SDS), but his trunk was relatively short (sitting height/height ratio -2.0 SDS). His gait was slightly abnormal and he could not run easily. He sustained a forearm fracture at 8 years. DEXA at 13 years showed BMD Z-scores of 0.2 in the lumbar spine and -2.1 in the proximal femur. Puberty began at 11.5 years, when his bone age was more than 1 year advanced. His cognitive development was above average and he had no epilepsy. However, he had autistic features, including difficulty with social communication, restricted behaviors and interests, sensitivity to environmental changes, and rigid thinking, which frequently led to panic attacks and school absenteeism. He had no joint pain, visual or hearing complaints, or skin abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Tise et al. (2025) reported 5 children from 4 families. All came to medical attention because of concern about short stature, and all had scoliosis and/or skeletal dysplasia. Proband 1 was a 3-year-old boy of European ancestry born to nonconsanguineous parents. He had bilateral developmental hip dysplasia, which was braced until age 9 months, and came to attention at age 2 years with increasing hip pain. He had proportionate short stature (z-score below -2 SD) and mild dysmorphic features: epicanthal folds, a flattened nasal bridge, and a short, anteverted nose. He also had tapered fingers and deep-set nails of the halluces. Pelvic x-rays showed delayed, stippled femoral ossification consistent with multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. A spine x-ray showed mild anterior beaking of the lumbar vertebrae.

paragraphs.text: Tise et al. (2025) also described fraternal twins (proband 3, male; proband 4, female) born at 34 weeks to nonconsanguineous parents. Their skeletal surveys showed spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia, which had been interpreted as consistent with Kniest dysplasia. Proband 3 had exaggerated thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis, anterior beaking of the vertebrae, short and broad femoral necks, and metaphyseal flaring. His scoliosis progressed from 12 degrees at age 4 years to an S-shaped 28-degree thoracic curve at 13 years. He also had pectus carinatum, a type 1 Chiari malformation, an atrial septal defect, and broad toes. Proband 4 had ovoid vertebrae with anterior wedging and widened metaphyses, along with broad thumbs, 2-3 toe syndactyly, and short, broad halluces. At age 10 years, their heights were 129.6 cm (z = -1.66) and 134.4 cm (z = -0.85), respectively.

paragraphs.text: Tise et al. (2025) built a homology model of SLC13A1 based on the SLC13A5 structure. The model predicted the following effects: R237C loses most contacts and hydrogen bonds at the intracellular end of transmembrane domain 5; G448D introduces clashes within transmembrane domain 9; L516P removes contacts and introduces clashes in transmembrane domain 10, part of the ligand recognition pocket; and Y582H removes nearly all contacts in the extracellular C terminus. In stably transfected MDCK cells, each of the missense variants R237C, G448D, L516P, and Y582H completely abolished [35S]-sulfate uptake. Each variant protein still reached the plasma membrane at levels similar to wildtype, suggesting that the substitutions impair transport without abolishing trafficking.

(2025) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the SLC13A1 gene by trio exome sequencing: a maternally inherited c.1343G-A transition, resulting in a gly448-to-asp (G448D) substitution, and a paternally inherited R12X mutation. paragraphs.text: In a girl of Asian ancestry with HSSD (proband 2) born to nonconsanguineous parents, Tise et al. (2025) identified a homozygous c.1744T-C transition in the SLC13A1 gene, resulting in a tyr582-to-his (Y582H) substitution, inherited from both parents. The mutation was found by targeted analysis of genome sequencing data. It was absent in the homozygous state from gnomAD v4.1.0, with 3 heterozygous alleles. The patient had a plasma sulfate of 0.107 mM (reference 0.3-0.5 mM) and an increased fractional excretion of sulfate. Homology modeling predicted that the substitution removes nearly all contacts in the extracellular C terminus. In MDCK cells, Y582H completely abolished sulfate transport but did not prevent trafficking to the plasma membrane.
